      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Surgery</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1">Operation</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Second Opinion</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>There are many reasons to have <span class="qt1">surgery. Some operations</span> can relieve or prevent pain. Others can reduce a symptom of a problem or improve some body function. Some <span class="qt1">surgeries</span> are done to find a problem. For example, a <span class="qt1">surgeon</span> may do a biopsy, which involves removing a piece of tissue to examine under a microscope. Some <span class="qt1">surgeries</span>, like heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span>, can save your life.</p><p>Some <span class="qt1">operations</span> that once needed large incisions (cuts in the body) can now be done using much smaller cuts. This is called laparoscopic <span class="qt1">surgery. Surgeons</span> insert a thin tube with a camera to see, and use small tools to do the <span class="qt1">surgery</span>.</p><p>After <span class="qt1">surgery</span> there can be a risk of complications, including infection, too much bleeding, reaction to anesthesia, or accidental injury. There is almost always some pain with <span class="qt1">surgery</span>.</p><p>Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality</p></content>

      <content name="title">Anesthesia</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is anesthesia?<p>Anesthesia is the use of medicines, called anesthetics, to prevent pain during <span class="qt1">surgery</span> and other medical procedures. Medicine may be given by injection, inhalation, topical lotion, spray, eye drops, or a skin patch.</p><p>Anesthesia can cause a loss of feeling, awareness, or both. Sedation may be used with anesthesia. Unlike full anesthesia, sedation doesn't make you completely unconscious, and recovery is faster. It helps reduce pain, keep you calm, and make you less aware during procedures such as minor <span class="qt1">surgeries</span>, endoscopies, imaging, or dental work.</p><p>Levels of sedation include:</p><ul><li>Minimal sedation. You are awake but more relaxed.</li><li>Moderate sedation (conscious sedation). You may feel sleepy and not remember much, but you can still respond when spoken to or touched.</li><li>Deep sedation. You are very drowsy and may respond only to repeated or stronger stimulation.</li></ul>What is anesthesia used for?<p>Anesthesia may be used for:</p><ul><li>Minor procedures, such as filling a tooth.</li><li>Childbirth or procedures such as colonoscopies.</li><li>Minor and major <span class="qt1">surgeries</span>.</li></ul><p>In some cases, a dentist, nurse, or doctor may give you an anesthetic. In other cases, you may need an anesthesiologist. This is a doctor who specializes in giving anesthesia.</p>What are the types of anesthesia?<p>There are several different types of anesthesia:</p><ul><li>Local anesthesia numbs a small area like a tooth or a cut that needs stitches.  You are awake during local anesthesia.</li><li>Regional anesthesia numbs a larger area, like an arm, a leg, or everything below the waist. You may be awake during the procedure, or you may be given sedation. It may be used during childbirth, a Cesarean delivery (C-section), or minor <span class="qt1">surgeries</span>.</li><li><span class="qt0">General</span> anesthesia affects your whole body. It feels like a deep sleep, but you do not feel anything. It is used during major <span class="qt1">surgeries</span>, such as heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span>, brain <span class="qt1">surgery</span>, back <span class="qt1">surgery</span>, and organ transplants.</li><li>Monitored sedation makes you relaxed or sleepy. You may be able to talk, depending on the level of sedation, and you probably won't remember the procedure. It may be used for a colonoscopy or dental work.</li></ul><p>Your overall health, medical history, the procedure you're having, and other factors will help determine the type of anesthesia you receive.</p>What are the risks of anesthesia?<p>Anesthesia is generally safe. But there can be risks, especially with <span class="qt0">general</span> anesthesia, including:</p><ul><li>Heart rhythm problem (arrhythmia).</li><li>Breathing problems.</li><li>An allergic reaction to the anesthesia.</li><li>Temporary confusion (delirium), which can last several days in some people over the age of 60, or briefly in children after waking up from anesthesia.</li><li>Awareness when someone is under <span class="qt0">general</span> anesthesia. This usually means that the person hears sounds. But sometimes they can feel pain. This is rare.</li></ul><p>Talk to your health care provider about the benefits and risks of anesthesia.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hysterectomy.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Hysterectomy</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is a <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span>?<p>A <span class="qt1">hysterectomy is surgery</span> to remove the uterus (womb). The uterus is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy. A <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> treats problems like heavy bleeding, pain, or cancer in the uterus.</p><p>After a <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span>, you no longer have menstrual periods and can't become pregnant. Sometimes the <span class="qt1">surgery</span> also removes the ovaries and fallopian tubes. If you have both ovaries taken out,menopause symptoms will usually begin.</p>What conditions does a <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> treat?<p><span class="qt1">Hysterectomy</span> is a major <span class="qt1">surgery</span>. Your health care provider may suggest other treatment options first. These might include medicine, hormone therapy, or procedures to remove fibroids or stop heavy bleeding. Sometimes these won't help, or <span class="qt1">surgery</span> might be the only option, depending on the condition that needs to be treated.</p><p>Your provider might recommend a <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> if you have:</p><ul><li>Fibroids, if you are near or past menopause, have large fibroids or very heavy bleeding.</li><li>Endometriosis, that hasn't been cured by medicine or <span class="qt1">surgery</span>.</li><li>Uterine prolapse, which can happen after several vaginal births, menopause, or because of obesity. It is when the uterus drops into the vagina.</li><li>Cancer, of the uterus, cervix, ovaries, or endometrium (the lining of the uterus).</li><li>Vaginal bleeding, that is heavy or unusual and persists despite treatment.</li><li>Chronic pelvic pain, which starts in the uterus. A <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> is a last resort since it doesn't fix some pelvic pain.</li><li>Adenomyosis, is a thickening of the walls of the uterus. A <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> is only considered if pain is severe and no other treatments have worked.</li></ul>What are the different types of <span class="qt1">hysterectomies</span>?<p>Your provider will discuss the type of <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> you need, depending on your condition.</p><p>The different types of <span class="qt1">surgeries</span> include:</p><ul><li>A total <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> is the most common type and involves the removal of all the uterus, including the cervix. The ovaries and fallopian tubes may or may not be removed.</li><li>A partial (subtotal or supracervical) <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> removes just the upper part of the uterus. The cervix is left in place, and your ovaries may or may not be removed</li><li>A radical <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> removes all the uterus, cervix, and tissue on both sides of the cervix and the upper part of the vagina. This is most often used to treat certain types of cancer, such as cervical cancer. The fallopian tubes and ovaries may or may not be removed.</li></ul>What methods are used for a <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span>?<p>A <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> may be done several different ways. Your provider will determine the best method for the <span class="qt1">surgery</span> based on your <span class="qt0">general</span> health, the reason for the <span class="qt1">surgery</span>, and other factors.</p><p>Methods to perform a <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span> include:</p><ul><li>Abdominal <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span>. A cut is made in your lower abdomen (belly). Your provider may recommend this method if you have a large uterus or to check other pelvic organs for signs of disease. This <span class="qt1">surgery</span> has a longer recovery time than the others.</li><li>Vaginal <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span>. A small cut is made in your vagina. This may not be an option if you have very large fibroids.</li><li>Laparoscopic <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span>. Uses an instrument with a thin, lighted tube and an attached camera. This helps your provider see your pelvic organs. Small cuts are made in either your abdomen (belly) or vagina. This is not an option for all types of uterine fibroids.</li><li>Robotic <span class="qt1">surgery</span>. Your provider guides a robotic arm to do the <span class="qt1">surgery</span> through small cuts in your lower abdomen (belly).</li></ul><p>After a <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span>, it can take four to six weeks to recover, depending on the type of <span class="qt1">surgery</span> you have.</p>What are the risks of a <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span>?<p>Like all <span class="qt1">surgeries, a hysterectomy</span> has risks, even though the results are usually good. Talk to your provider about the benefits and risks of having a <span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span>.</p><p>More serious risks can include:</p><ul><li>Too much bleeding during <span class="qt1">surgery</span></li><li>Infection</li><li>Blood clots</li></ul><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/heartvalvediseases.html">
      <content name="title">Heart Valve Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Aortic Stenosis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Heart Murmur</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Valvular Heart Diseases</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Valvular heart disease</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are heart valve diseases?<p>Heart valve disease happens when one or more of your heart valves don't work well.</p><p>Your heart has four valves: the tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, and aortic valves. The valves have flaps that open and close. The flaps make sure that blood flows in the right direction through your heart and to the rest of your body. When your heart beats, the flaps open to let blood through. Between heartbeats they close to stop the blood from flowing backwards.</p><p>If one or more of your heart valves doesn't open or close correctly, it can affect your blood flow and strain your heart. Fortunately, treatment helps most valve diseases.</p>What are the types of heart valve diseases?<p>Heart valves can have three basic kinds of problems:</p><ul><li>Regurgitation, or backflow, happens when the flaps of a valve don't close tightly. This allows the blood to leak backwards. A common cause of regurgitation is prolapse, where the flaps of the valve flop or bulge back. Prolapse most often affects the mitral valve.</li><li>Stenosis happens when the flaps of a valve become thick, stiff, or stuck together. This prevents the heart valve from opening all the way. Not enough blood can pass through the valve. Aortic valve stenosis is a common type of stenosis. It affects the valve that controls blood flow into the large artery that carries blood out of the heart to the body.</li><li>Atresia happens when a heart valve did not form properly and does not have an opening for blood to pass through.</li></ul><p>Sometimes a valve can have both regurgitation and stenosis.</p>What causes heart valve diseases?<p>Some people are born with heart valve disease. This is called congenital heart valve disease. It can happen alone or along with other congenital heart defects. Heart valve disease can also develop over time as you get older or have certain conditions that affect the heart.</p>Who is more likely to develop heart valve diseases?<p>Your chance of having heart valve disease is higher if:</p><ul><li>You are older. With age, the heart valves can become thick and stiff.</li><li>You have or have had other conditions that affect your heart and blood vessels. These include:
	<ul><li>Rheumatic fever. An untreated strep throat can become rheumatic fever, which can harm the heart valves. The damage may not show up for years. Today, most people take antibiotics to cure strep throat before it can cause heart valve damage.</li><li>Endocarditis. This is a rare infection in the lining of the heart and heart valves. It is usually caused by bacteria in the bloodstream.</li><li>A heart attack.</li><li>Heart failure.</li><li>Coronary artery disease, especially when it affects the aorta (the large artery that carries blood from the heart to the body).</li><li>High blood pressure.</li><li>High blood cholesterol.</li><li>Diabetes.</li><li>Obesity and overweight.</li><li>Lack of physical activity.</li></ul>
</li><li>A family history of early heart disease:<ul><li>A father or brother who had heart disease younger than 55.</li><li>A mother or sister who had heart disease younger than 65.</li></ul></li><li>You were born with an aortic valve that wasn't formed right. Sometimes this will cause problems right away. Other times, the valve may work well enough for years before causing problems.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of heart valve diseases?<p>Many people live their whole lives with a heart valve that doesn't work perfectly and never have any problems. But heart valve disease may get worse slowly over time. You may develop signs and symptoms, such as:</p><ul><li>Shortness of breath (feeling like you can't get enough air)</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Swelling in your feet, ankles, abdomen (belly), or the veins in your neck</li><li>Chest pain when you're physically active</li><li>Arrhythmia, a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat</li><li>Dizziness or fainting</li></ul><p>If you don't get treatment for heart valve disease, the symptoms and strain on your heart may keep getting worse.</p>What other problems can heart valve diseases cause?<p>When the valves don't work well, your heart has to pump harder to get enough blood out to the body.  Without treatment, this extra workload on your heart can lead to:</p><ul><li>Heart failure</li><li>Stroke</li><li>Blood clots</li><li>Sudden cardiac arrest or death</li></ul>How is heart valve disease diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may listen to your heart with a stethoscope and hear that your heart makes abnormal sounds, such as a click or a heart murmur. These sounds may mean a valve isn't working normally. The provider will usually refer you to a cardiologist, a doctor who specializes in heart diseases.</p><p>The doctor will also listen to your heart and will do a physical exam. You will also likely need to have one or more heart tests.</p>What are the treatments for heart valve diseases?<p>Most heart valve problems can be treated successfully. Treatment may include:</p><ul><li>Medicines to control your symptoms and keep your heart pumping well</li><li>Heart-healthy lifestyle changes to treat other related heart conditions</li><li><span class="qt1">Surgery</span> to repair or replace a valve</li></ul><p>It's possible that you may need <span class="qt1">surgery</span>, even if you don't have symptoms. Fixing the valve can help prevent future heart problems.</p><p>There are many ways to do heart valve <span class="qt1">surgery</span>. You and your doctor can decide what's best for you, based on your valve problem and <span class="qt0">general</span> health. Heart valve repair <span class="qt1">surgery</span> has fewer risks than heart valve replacement. So, when repair is possible, it's preferred over valve replacement.</p><p>In some cases, valve replacement is necessary. There are 2 types of replacement valves:</p><ul><li>Biologic valves made from pig, cow, or human tissue. These valves tend to wear out after 10 to 15 years, but some may last longer.</li><li>Mechanical (human-made) valves usually don't wear out. But with a mechanical valve, you usually have to take blood thinners for the rest of your life to prevent blood clots. And your risk of endocarditis (a heart infection) is higher than with a biologic valve.</li></ul><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/heartsurgery.html">
      <content name="title">Heart <span class="qt1">Surgery</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cardiac <span class="qt1">Surgery</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Open Heart <span class="qt1">Surgery</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span>?<p>Heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> can correct certain heart problems when other treatments haven't worked or can't be used.</p><p>In some cases, heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> may be a medical emergency. For example, <span class="qt1">surgery</span> for a severe heart attack may need to be done right away. In other cases, you can plan heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> ahead of time. Some heart <span class="qt1">surgeries</span> are major <span class="qt1">operations</span>, such as heart bypass <span class="qt1">surgery</span> for blocked arteries in the heart. Other <span class="qt1">surgeries</span> are more minor heart procedures, such as putting in a pacemaker.</p>What conditions does heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> treat?<p>There are different types of heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> that can help treat many heart conditions:</p>What conditions does heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> treat?What does the heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> do?Coronary artery disease (CAD) - when a sticky substance called plaque narrows or blocks the arteries that supply blood to your heart muscle.Makes a new path for blood to flow around the blocked part of an artery in the heart. This is called a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG), or heart bypass. It's the most common heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> in adults.Heart valve diseases - problems with the valves that control the flow of blood through your heart.Repairs heart valves.Replaces heart valves with a mechanical valve or a biologic valve made from pig, cow, or human heart tissue.Arrhythmia - problems with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat. They are caused by changes in the electrical signals that control your heartbeat.Places a pacemaker or an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) in the chest to correct your heartbeat.Treats atrial fibrillation with small cuts in the heart muscle. The cuts form scars that make a path for the heart's electrical signals (Maze <span class="qt1">surgery</span>).Heart failure - when your heart is too weak or stiff to pump enough oxygen-rich blood to meet your body's needs.Places a device in the chest which may include:<ul><li>An implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) to help prevent sudden cardiac arrest.</li><li>A biventricular pacemaker to coordinate the heart's pumping action so it's more powerful.</li><li>A ventricular assist device to help the heart pump blood.</li><li>A total artificial heart to pump blood for the heart.</li></ul>Replaces a seriously diseased heart with a heathy heart (heart transplantation).Heart aneurysm - a balloon-like bulge in the wall of an artery. It can be life-threatening if the aneurysm tears or bursts.Repairs or replaces the weak part of a heart artery using a patch or a tube made of fabric.Angina - chest pain from coronary artery disease.Uses a laser to make small channels through part of the heart muscle (transmyocardial laser revascularization).Damaged and abnormal heart structures, including congenital heart defects - heart structure problems that you're born with.Repairs heart damage or problems with how the heart and blood vessels are formed. Repairs depend on the type of defect or damage.What approaches do <span class="qt1">surgeons</span> use to do heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span>?<p>The approach a <span class="qt1">surgeon</span> uses to do heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> depends on your heart problem, your <span class="qt0">general</span> health, and other factors. Approaches to heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> include:</p><ul><li>Open-heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> (also called traditional heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span>) is when the <span class="qt1">surgeon</span> cuts the chest open to reach the heart. Because it's difficult to operate on a beating heart, medicines are used to stop the heart. A heart-lung bypass machine keeps oxygen-rich blood pumping through the body during the <span class="qt1">surgery</span>.</li><li>Off-pump heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> is open-heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> on a beating heart without using a heart-lung bypass machine. The <span class="qt1">surgeon</span> holds the heart steady with a device. <span class="qt1">Surgeons</span> may use off-pump heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> to do coronary artery bypass grafts (CABG), but only in certain cases.</li><li>Minimally invasive heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> uses small cuts between the ribs. The cuts may be as small as 2 to 3 inches. The <span class="qt1">surgeon</span> inserts tools into the chest through the cuts. This type of heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> may or may not use a heart-lung bypass machine.</li><li>Robotic-assisted <span class="qt1">surgery</span> is a type of minimally invasive <span class="qt1">surgery. The surgeon</span> uses a computer to control tools on the arms of a robot. This allows the <span class="qt1">surgeon</span> to be very accurate when doing difficult <span class="qt1">operations</span>.</li></ul>What are the risks of heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span>?<p>Like all <span class="qt1">surgery</span>, heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> has risks even though the results are often excellent. The risks include:</p><ul><li>Bleeding</li><li>Infection, fever, and swelling</li><li>A problem from anesthesia (medicine that makes you sleep during <span class="qt1">surgery</span>)</li><li>Arrhythmia</li><li>Damage to the heart, kidneys, liver, and lungs</li><li>Stroke</li></ul><p>The risks of heart <span class="qt1">surgery</span> tend to be higher if:</p><ul><li>The <span class="qt1">surgery</span> is an emergency.</li><li>You have other medical conditions, including:
	<ul><li>Diabetes</li><li>Kidney diseases</li><li>Lung diseases</li><li>Peripheral artery disease (PAD)</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>
